purpose: Gabapentin is used to help control certain types of seizures in people with epilepsy. It is also used to relieve nerve pain, such as the burning or shooting pain that can happen after a shingles infection. Sometimes doctors prescribe it for other types of nerve-related pain or conditions like restless leg syndrome.
how_it_works: Gabapentin works by calming down overactive nerve signals in your brain and throughout your body. Think of it like a volume knob — it turns down the extra electrical activity in your nerves that causes seizures or pain. It does this by affecting certain channels in nerve cells that control how signals are sent and received.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include feeling drowsy or dizzy, especially when you first start taking it. You might also notice feeling tired, having trouble with coordination or balance, and blurred vision. Some people experience swelling in their hands or feet, or mild memory or concentration issues.
warnings: Gabapentin can make you very drowsy, so do not drive or use heavy machinery until you know how it affects you. Do not stop taking it suddenly — always talk to your doctor first, as stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms or increase your risk of seizures. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted. There is also a risk of breathing problems if taken with opioids, alcohol, or other sedating medicines, which can be very dangerous.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very individual and depends on what condition is being treated. For nerve pain, adults often start at a low dose like 300 mg once a day and slowly increase to 300–600 mg taken three times a day. For seizures, doses can be higher. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribed, and try to space your doses evenly throughout the day.
